paras: The lynching of William Williams was the shooting of a Black labor agent by a crowd in Centerville, Mississippi, on September 15, 1903, shortly after he shot and killed James H. Germany, a white employee of the Robinson Mercantile Company. Wire reports put the mob at several hundred people. Mississippi papers treated the killing as an episode in a seasonal conflict over labor agents who drew Black workers away from local employers, while a Black weekly read it as punishment for encouraging Black workers to leave for better wages.

Williams had spent several days in Centerville hiring Black workers for contractors elsewhere, "in other states" in the Associated Press version and in other parts of Mississippi in a Houston Post special. He was alleged to have induced several employees of the Robinson Mercantile Company to leave the firm, and the New York Sun's New Orleans dispatch said he had persuaded hands to break their contracts.

Germany met Williams on the street and remonstrated with him about the workers; the Sun called Germany a manager of the company, other reports an employee. According to the white papers, a quarrel followed in which Williams drew a revolver and fired three shots, the first of which killed Germany in front of the Robinson store on Main street.

Williams then ran, and a crowd drawn by the shots pursued him down the street. The Oxford Eagle said a "general melee" began once Williams left the crowded Main street, with Williams returning fire as he ran. He was shot to death by his pursuers; the Associated Press said he was first "captured," and the Indianapolis Freeman that he was "shot to pieces."

The Oxford Eagle reported that everything was quiet and no further trouble was expected, and that Germany left a wife and five children. No report of an inquest, arrests, a grand jury inquiry or any official response was found, and no member of the crowd was named.

The Associated Press dispatch, dated Centerville, September 15, ran on September 16 from Richmond to San Francisco under headlines such as "Lynched by a Mob" and "Killed a White Man and Was Soon Lynched." The Savannah Morning News headed it "Mob in Centerville, Miss., Quickly Avenged Germany," and the Houston Post special, reprinted in two Texas papers, ran under the subhead "Negro Str[u]ng Up by a Mob of Irate Mississippi," though its text described a shooting.

The Sun's separate New Orleans dispatch avoided the word "lynched" and headed its story "Negro Murderer Shot Down." Mississippi papers wrote from the side of the dead white man: the Brookhaven Leader called Williams "a worthless negro" and "the murderer," and a paragraph titled "Rapid Action," run in at least seven Mississippi weeklies, remarked on his "poor marksmanship." The Columbus Commercial set the killing among the fall "labor troubles" brought on by out-of-state agents, saying only that "the negro was promptly lynched," and the Hattiesburg Daily Progress said the enticing of labor alone had not caused the lynching.

Two Black weeklies took up the story days later; the Indianapolis Freeman followed the wire account in two sentences, writing that Williams was "shot to pieces." The Seattle Republican, without naming Williams or the town, wrote that the man's "primal offense" was trying to induce Black workers "to go where they could get more wages," that the white man had "no doubt" objected to his influencing "our niggers" to leave, and that Williams fired in self-defense, concluding that the South meant to keep Black people "in ignorance and servitude."

Accounts differ on where and how Williams died: the Associated Press said he was captured and then shot in Main street, while the Sun and the Oxford Eagle placed his death at the edge of town during the chase. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress said a committee of citizens had ordered Williams to leave and a mob lynched him when he stayed, after he had killed the white man "the day before"; the item also put Centerville in Texas, while the dated dispatches place both killings on one day. Every white account has Williams firing first after Germany remonstrated, while the Seattle Republican, without citing a source, inferred that he acted in self-defense.

reader.title: Lynching of William Williams
bases: A crowd of several hundred chased and shot to death Williams after he was accused of killing a white man; the wire called it a lynching (A1, A10, A21).

Williams was shot to death by 'a mob of several hundred people' with no lawful authority mentioned (A1, A10), in retaliation for the shooting of Germany, which a headline called avenging him (A9); the Sun called it shooting down a murderer (A13).

The AP wire (A1), a Houston Post special (A10), a separate New Orleans dispatch (A13) and a Mississippi state paragraph (A21) agree that Williams shot Germany and was chased and shot to death by a crowd.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Williams shot Germany in a quarrel; a mob of several hundred chased him in a running fight, captured him and shot him to death on Main street.

accounts.label: Houston Post special
accounts.gist: Adds that Williams allegedly enticed Robinson Mercantile Co. employees and that Germany, a white employee, met and remonstrated with him before the shooting.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: Germany, a manager, warned Williams that taking hands was ruinous; Williams fired three shots, fled firing, and was brought down by a volley at the town line; not called a lynching.

accounts.label: Mississippi state paragraph ('Rapid Action')
accounts.gist: Crowd could not fire on crowded Main street; Williams returned fire while fleeing and was overtaken before the town limits and riddled with bullets.

accounts.label: Hattiesburg Daily Progress editorial
accounts.gist: A citizens' committee ordered Williams to leave; a mob caught and lynched him when he did not, after he had killed the white man the day before.

accounts.label: Black editor (Seattle Republican)
accounts.gist: Lynched for trying to take Black workers to better wages; the white man objected and Williams shot him in self-defense (the editor's inference).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Freeman
accounts.gist: Williams shot Germany in an altercation and was shot to pieces by a mob after a running fight.
